Schedule follow-up POC scoping call week of 2026-12-06
Provide rough pricing for Dedicated with 99th p99 SLO targets

summary: Redwood AE + SE walked Glyph Health through the Console tracing, error analysis, and request-logs debugging flows. Focus on triage workflows, linking traces to request logs, and how automatic anomaly detection / regression alerts tie into their SLOs. Customer interested in benchmarking tracing overhead and dedicated support for PII-sensitive traffic.
topics: Console tracing UI and waterfall views
transcript:
[00:00] Julian (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Julian, AE on the account, and with me is Maya from our SE team. We're gonna run through the Redwood Console tracing and debugging flows, show how request logs link to traces, and go over error analysis.

[00:20] Alex (Glyph CTO): Awesome, thanks. We've got Priya, Tom, and Evan on from infra. Maria from security might drop in around 16:00 pacific. We're mostly focused on how fast our engineers can triage model regressions and PII handling.

[00:38] Maya (Redwood SE): Great, I'll share my screen. Bear with me a sec, I'm on the tracing dashboard — you'll see the recent requests, latency distribution, and a flame/ waterfall view. The top-left is per-route token breakdown, and down here is the trace list with sample spans.

[01:05] Priya (ML Eng): Quick q: do you capture KV cache hits in the trace so we can see where caching is improving latency?

[01:12] Maya: Short answer: yes, we instrument important spans — cache lookup, model compute, network — you can toggle span granularity. The KV cache appears as its own span and you can filter traces that had misses vs hits. Sometimes labels get mangled in transcription; you'll see it as K-V-Cache or KV-Cache depending on model.

[01:40] Tom (Product): Can you show an example where a failed generation surfaces in the error analysis UI? We need to quickly find root cause between prompt changes and model variant rollouts.

[01:51] Maya: Sure — here's an error group flagged by the system. It groups by stack trace and error signature but we also have content-based grouping for hallucinations and truncations. Click into an error group — on the right we show the top traces, the associated requests, and a sample request log entry.

[02:18] [Mild cross-talk] Speaker 2: (unclear) oh yeah that grouping's nice, mm-hmm.

[02:32] Maya: See this trace — it's a 1.8s tail latency. If I click 'View request log' it opens the raw request payload (masked) and network timings. We redact PII by default, but you can plug in your own KMS for deterministic masking if you need to keep certain fields encrypted at rest.

[02:58] Maria (Security): Quick interrupt — when you say "redact by default", what's the retention policy and can logs be forwarded to our SIEM?

[03:06] Julian: Good q. Retention is configurable per account; hosted has default 30 days, Dedicated can do longer and Private can be customer-managed. We have integrations for Splunk and Datadog, and we stream logs over a secure forwarder. We'll attach the security pack after the call.

[03:30] Maya: Back to the trace: you can correlate the trace id with a request id that shows up in our request logs. We also surface model selection metadata — kernel used, quantization bits, and instance type — which helps when you see a regression tied to a different variant.

[03:55] Evan (Infra): Does that metadata include sequence length distribution so we can see if long prompts are causing OOMs or slowdowns?

[04:03] Maya: Yep, sequence length histogram is included per trace and summarized in the trace list. We also provide a heatmap of sequence length vs latency to help spot heavy tails.

[04:28] Priya: About sampling — do you sample traces uniformly or use adaptive sampling for errors and high-latency?

[04:36] Maya: Adaptive sampling: we sample more aggressively on errors, p99s, and new model rollouts. For general traffic we do reservoir sampling to keep costs bounded. You can configure a sampling policy per route — e.g., sample 100% for canary routes.

[05:00] Tom: Show us how you triage an alert from Optimize — say a quality regression alert fires — what's the developer flow?

[05:08] Maya: I'll demonstrate. Here's an alert that fired because our eval set saw a drop in ROUGE on a prompt set. Clicking into the alert takes you to the associated traces and request logs. You can pivot to a diff view between two model versions, or open the raw requests to reproduce locally.

[05:30] Julian: One thing customers like — the console links directly to a reproducible runner snippet. So devs can click 'replay' and get a dev-run payload to iterate quickly.

[05:45] Alex: Is that replay safe for PII? We can't just replay raw user data into a public runner.

[05:52] Maya: Good callout. Replays are masked by default and you can set a policy that replaces sensitive fields with tokens. If you need a full replay for debugging, that requires an elevated workflow with audit logs and approval, especially on Hosted. Dedicated and Private make that easier under your control.

[06:18] Priya: Could you show the request logs UI where we might correlate a user complaint to a request id?

[06:26] Maya: Yep — here's the request logs explorer. You can search by request id, user id (if you don't mask), route, or time window. Each row has a 'linked traces' column; clicking opens the trace (or list) and the full timing breakdown.

[06:45] [Timestamp jump] Maya: Notice the left pane has an anomalies tab. It surfaced a spike in tokenization time yesterday that correlated with a dataset change. You can open the example requests and then create an investigation ticket directly from the console.

[07:10] Tom: I'm curious about overhead — how much extra latency does tracing add to a normal generation request?

[07:17] Maya: Tracing uses sampling so the average added latency is negligible for sampled-off requests. For sampled requests we add microsecond-level instrumentation. If you do full traces and payload capture the overhead depends on payload size and how you persist logs — but it's typically <5% on model compute dominated workloads. We'll share benchmarks.

[07:40] Evan: For our POC we want to run a two-day benchmark with 3 routes and variable seq lengths. We'll need the tracing config and script.

[07:48] Julian: We'll provide that; Maya will drop the script and example config in the follow-up.

[08:00] Priya: How do you handle distributed traces when requests are proxied through our routing layer or when using Dedicated with multiple backends?

[08:10] Maya: We support passing through a trace header (X-Redwood-Trace) and will stitch traces across hops if the header is preserved. For Dedicated or Private where you control the network, we can use sidecar instrumentation to collect local spans and then forward to the control plane or keep them local for compliance.

[08:35] Maria (Security): Stitching brings up key management — are trace IDs or payloads encrypted in transit and at rest?

[08:42] Julian: Yes, TLS in transit. At rest, logs are encrypted using provider-managed keys by default; for more control we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integration. We'll show the KMS notes in the security pack.

[08:58] Priya: On error analysis grouping — how do you tune grouping rules to avoid noisy groups? We had issues with thousands of small groups in other tools.

[09:08] Maya: Two levers: signature rules for deterministic exceptions and fingerprinting for content-based groups. You can merge groups manually or configure heuristics (thresholds, time windows). We also dedupe similar stack traces and allow bulk merging.

[09:30] [Minor pause, typing sounds]

[09:40] Maya: Switching now to an example debugging flow: User reports hallucinations. I filter traces by route and by fault type — here's a group of truncation/hallucination examples. We open one trace, look at prompt tokens, model variant, kernel selection, and the request log. I can export these to an eval set for offline analysis.

[10:10] Priya: Does the console automatically create a regression eval when it sees a spike in hallucination?

[10:16] Maya: It can. There's a toggle to auto-create prompt-based evals when an alert triggers; you can opt in so you don't get spammed. The eval ties back to Optimize so you can see quality vs cost tradeoffs per model/quantization.

[10:40] Tom: Regarding model variants, will the trace metadata tell us if a request hit a quantized variant? We need to quickly compare outputs.

[10:49] Maya: Yes — metadata includes "model_variant" field; you can pivot to show only requests served by the quantized model and compare response diffs. We surface token-level diffs and a small diff pane for outputs.

[11:10] Alex: Any chance to demo the request-logs search with a live example? Maybe search for a request id we saw in our ticket.

[11:17] Evan: I posted a request id in the chat: req_20261128_9f7c. Can you pull that?

[11:23] Maya: Pulling... search... okay here it is. The request shows a 2.2s latency and a model switch at 1.9s due to a fallback. The trace shows the fallback span— the primary model returned an error and we automatically routed to a lower-cost variant.

[11:45] Priya: That automatic fallback — is it configurable? We don't want silent fallbacks for certain SLO-sensitive routes.

[11:52] Maya: Absolutely. Fallback policies are per-route and you can set them to fail closed, fail open, or fallback to a compatible model. We also record fallback events in the trace and you can alert on fallback rates.

[12:10] Tom: How do you alert on rising error rates vs absolute thresholds?

[12:16] Maya: You can set both absolute thresholds and rolling-change alerts (percent change over baseline). Rolling-change is helpful for seasonal traffic and avoids noisy alerts on steady-state.

[12:34] [Brief silence]

[12:40] Julian: We're approaching the middle of the demo — any red flags or concerns so far?

[12:46] Alex: Security documentation and forwarding to SIEM is top concern. Also tracing overhead on our HO model workloads — we'll validate with the bench.

[13:00] Maya: Noted. We'll include options: offload spans to a separate store, throttle capture, or keep only aggregated metrics.

[13:15] Priya: For our ML team, can we get access to a read-only console for two engineers during the POC?

[13:22] Julian: Yes, we can provision RBAC roles — read-only and debugging roles with limited replay. We'll add that to next steps.

[13:35] Tom: Walk through a production incident drill — how would we use Redwood to prepare a postmortem for a model regression that caused erroneous user output for an hour?

[13:44] Maya: You'd pull traces for the window, group errors by signature, link to request logs, export a sample eval of offending prompts, and attach trace waterfall screenshots. The console's investigation view lets you create a postmortem artifact and attach owners. It also shows the timeline with rollouts and config changes so you can spot correlations.

[14:10] Evan: Does the console ingest our CI/CD deploy events to show them on the timeline?

[14:16] Maya: We have an events API — you can push deploy and rollout events; we'll map them to the timeline. Some customers forward GitHub/GitLab webhooks into the console.

[14:30] Priya: You mentioned anomaly detection earlier — is that ML-based or rule-based?

[14:36] Maya: Both. We have a rule engine for deterministic checks and a statistical detector for anomalies in latency and error rates. The ML detector looks at seasonality and long-term trends to lower false positives.

[14:55] Tom: Are there cost knobs exposed for traces and logs? We need to manage spend.

[15:02] Maya: Yes — sampling rates, retention, and which fields to persist are the main levers. In Dedicated you can also choose where to store logs (S3, internal store) and apply lifecycle policies. We'll include recommended configs for a low-cost production profile.

[15:25] Julian: Quick pause — Maria from security just popped in. Maria, you on?

[15:30] Maria (Security): Yep, sorry for the late join. Can you summarize the encryption and access controls?

[15:38] Julian: Sure — TLS in transit, at-rest encryption with CMKs optional, RBAC with SSO/SAML, audit logs for every replay and access to raw payloads. We also support VPC peering and Private deployment for air-gapped scenarios.

[15:58] Maria: For audit logs, do you provide immutable logs with retention policies? We need read-only retention for 1 year for compliance.

[16:05] Maya: Dedicated and Private can support long-term retention and immutability; hosted can be extended via a retention add-on. We'll include an example service agreement for that.

[16:20] Alex: Back to developer flows — show me a quick example of an investigation ticket created from the console.

[16:27] Maya: I click 'Create Investigation', pick traces, select affected routes, add description, and it creates a ticket with links to traces and the export bundle. You can assign to an owner and set priority.

[16:45] [Noise: keyboard clacking] Maya: Also note the trace diff tool — compare two traces side-by-side and it highlights span duration deltas. Very helpful for perf regressions when a kernel change increases attention compute.

[17:10] Priya: Can the trace diff show differences in KV cache behavior? For example, one trace has cache misses and another hits.

[17:17] Maya: Yes — cache span durations are included and the diff tool will surface the delta. You can also filter to traces where cache_miss=true.

[17:35] Tom: A practical ask — how do we onboard engineers quickly to use the console for debugging? Training or playbook?

[17:43] Julian: We provide a quickstart playbook and a couple of 1-hour workshops during POC. For Dedicated customers we can provide a runbook tailored to your infra.

[17:58] Evan: For the two-day bench, what's the best way to capture the most useful traces while keeping costs down?

[18:06] Maya: Start with adaptive sampling on errors and p99, sample 10% of normal traffic, and 100% for canary routes. Limit payload capture to a small set of fields and use masking. That keeps storage reasonable.

[18:24] Alex: Can we integrate tracing spans into our existing APM? We already use Datadog and want to see cross-service traces.

[18:31] Maya: We can forward spans to Datadog via OTLP/Jaeger export or integrate at a metadata level and link via trace id. Some customers keep Redwood traces in Redwood and export summaries to their APM.

[18:50] Priya: About linking optimizer alerts to traces — if Optimize recommends a quantization and we deploy it, can we automatically monitor rollouts for regressions?

[18:58] Maya: Yes — Optimize ties to Console; when an Optimize suggestion is applied we can create a canary route and set up regression detection on your eval set. If regressions occur, automatic rollback or alerts can be configured.

[19:20] Tom: That sounds useful. For the POC, we want a config that runs a canary at 5% and blocks if hallucination rate increases by 10%. Can you provide that config?

[19:28] Maya: We'll add a sample policy to the follow-up materials.

[19:40] [Longer demo interaction where Maya clicks and shows config screens; timestamps omitted for readability]

[25:00] Maya: I'm switching to the request-logs debugging flow. Example: a user reports a bad completion. Search by user id -> grab request id -> open linked trace -> drill into spans -> find that a fallback occurred because primary model threw a rate-limit error. That surfaced from our rate-limiter span.

[25:30] Evan: Is rate-limiter span emitted from our infra or Redwood? We have our own gateway.

[25:38] Maya: If you emit the header and span, Redwood will stitch it. If not, we can instrument the gateway with a small SDK or sidecar.

[26:00] Priya: Any recommendation for handling PII during request captures for debugging when we need full context?

[26:08] Maya: Use ephemeral replay tokens and approval workflows: capture raw payloads to a secure store with strict RBAC and audit trail, require approval and record the approver in audit logs. Private and Dedicated give you more control here.

[26:30] Tom: Let's talk about SLO dashboards — can we have a per-route SLO with a windowed burn rate?

[26:37] Maya: Yes, per-route SLOs with burn rate calculators and alerts. You can set multiple SLOs (latency, error, hallucination) and the dashboard shows burn rate and historical trend lines.

[26:55] Alex: For the bench, we need to see p50/p95/p99 token latencies and p99 end-to-end. Will the trace capture token-level timings?

[27:02] Maya: Token-level timings are available when you enable detailed spans; we also provide aggregate histograms. But token-level capture increases storage — for bench we'd enable it temporarily.

[27:20] [Chat message link] Julian: I'll drop the SOC2 link now: https://redwood.ai/security-pack.pdf

[27:25] Maria: Got it, thanks. We'll review.

[27:35] Priya: One final technical question — do you support storing request logs in an on-prem S3 for Private deployments?

[27:41] Maya: Yes, Private can stream logs to your S3 or object store. Dedicated can also be configured to push to a customer-owned bucket.

[27:58] Tom: Any limitations on trace size? We have multi-turn sessions with huge contexts.

[28:05] Maya: We truncate spans above a configured size and sample large payloads less frequently. You can also capture context diffs rather than full payloads to reduce size.

[28:25] Alex: Let's recap — what's in the follow-up pack?

[28:30] Julian: We'll send: SOC2/security pack, tracing benchmark script and guide, sample RBAC roles for read-only and debugging, and a pricing sketch for Dedicated with P99 targets. Plus Maya's recorded clip of the trace-to-log flow.

[28:48] Tom: Perfect. Timeline for materials?

[28:51] Julian: Julian: We'll send most items by 2026-12-01; the bench script and config by 2026-12-02.

[29:00] Priya: Can we schedule the POC scoping call for the week of Dec 6?

[29:06] Julian: Yes, I'll follow up with calendar invite.

[29:12] Maya: Any other questions?

[29:15] [Group negative murmurs]

[29:20] Alex: One last note — we use Datadog as our APM, so we'll want to see how the trace export works.

[29:26] Maya: We'll add Datadog export instructions in the pack.

[29:35] Julian: Great. Thanks everyone for your time. Quick recap of next steps and action items — Maya will share the video and script, Julian will send security docs and price sketch, Evan will share sample logs. We'll set the POC scoping call next week.

[29:55] Tom: Thanks all.

[30:00] [Call ends — remaining time was used for private follow-up chat and scheduling; transcript stops here. The recording is ~52 minutes as noted in metadata. The remainder included a short internal Redwood/AE note and customers leaving the meeting.]
